notes.meaning: Pilate asked what crime Jesus had committed, seeing no legal basis under Roman law to condemn Him. Instead of answering with an actual charge, the angry crowd simply shouted louder for Him to be executed on a cross. Their reaction showed that Jesus was entirely innocent and that His death was driven by envy and hatred rather than justice.

Seeing that a riot was beginning and that his reasoning had no effect, Pilate washed his hands with water before the crowd. This was an ancient Jewish practice used to declare oneself free from the guilt of an unsolved murder. Pilate claimed to be innocent of Jesus' blood, but washing his hands could not excuse his failure to uphold justice.

The crowd recklessly shouted that the responsibility for Jesus' death should fall on them and their children. Commentators traditionally saw this fulfilled in the terrible judgment and suffering that fell upon Jerusalem when Roman armies destroyed it in AD 70. Yet God's mercy remained open, and Jesus' blood also brings forgiveness to all who turn to Him in repentance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that this shout represented the local crowd and pointed to the coming destruction of Jerusalem, rather than placing a perpetual curse on all Jewish people across history.

notes.meaning: Pilate freed the criminal Barabbas and ordered Jesus to be flogged, which was the brutal Roman custom before crucifixion. Soldiers whipped Him with leather straps embedded with sharp bone and metal fragments, tearing His flesh. Jesus was then handed over to die, taking the place of guilty sinners so they might be set free.

The Roman governor's soldiers escorted Jesus into the Praetorium, which was Pilate's official residence and headquarters in Jerusalem. There they assembled their whole cohort, a unit of hundreds of troops. They brought Him inside to mock and abuse Him away from the public eye.

The soldiers stripped Jesus of His outer garments and put a scarlet soldier's cloak around Him. This red cloak was meant to look like the expensive purple robes worn by kings and Roman generals. They used it to turn His claim of being a king into a cruel joke.

They twisted prickly thorn branches into a crown and pressed it onto His head, placing a wooden reed in His right hand like a king's staff. Then they fell on their knees before Him in mock respect, shouting, 'Hail, King of the Jews!' Though done in ridicule, their actions unknowingly pointed to the day when all people will bow before Him as the true King.

The soldiers spat on Jesus' face to show the deepest possible insult and contempt. They took the staff out of His hand and struck Him on the head repeatedly, driving the sharp thorns into His scalp. Through all this pain and shame, He offered no resistance and bore our punishment willingly.

When they finished making sport of Him, the soldiers removed the scarlet cloak and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him away to the execution site outside the city walls. He walked toward His death as a willing sacrifice, enduring humiliation to bring us life.

Along the road, the soldiers met Simon from Cyrene in North Africa and forced him to carry Jesus' heavy wooden cross. A condemned prisoner normally carried his own crossbeam, but Jesus was exhausted from the sleepless night and severe beatings. Simon was drafted into service, giving believers a vivid picture of taking up the cross to follow Christ.

The procession reached a place called Golgotha, an Aramaic word meaning 'The Place of the Skull.' It was a hill outside Jerusalem's walls, likely named for its rounded shape or because public executions took place there. Jesus was taken outside the city so that He could bring His people into God's eternal presence.

Before nailing Him to the cross, they offered Jesus sour wine mixed with bitter gall, a common drink intended to dull the pain. Jesus tasted it to acknowledge the offer, but He refused to drink it. He chose to remain fully conscious so He could experience the full weight of suffering for our sins.

The soldiers nailed Jesus to the wooden cross and divided His clothing among themselves by casting lots, like throwing dice. This fulfilled the ancient prophecy in Psalm 22:18, which foretold that the sufferer's garments would be divided. Jesus was stripped of everything so that we might be clothed in His grace.

After nailing Him to the cross, the soldiers sat down on the ground to stand guard over Him. They remained there to prevent friends or relatives from trying to rescue the prisoner before death. Indifferent to the significance of what was happening, they watched over the Saviour of the world as just another execution.

Roman authorities attached a written notice above Jesus' head detailing the official charge against Him: 'This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.' Pilate intended this notice as an explanation of the execution and a jab at the Jewish leadership. Yet God used this title to proclaim to all viewers that Jesus truly is the promised King.

Two violent robbers were crucified alongside Jesus, one placed on His right and the other on His left. Hanging between two common criminals added to His disgrace, making Him appear to be the worst offender of them all. This fulfilled the prophecy in Isaiah 53:12 that the Messiah would be counted among lawbreakers.

People walking by the cross shook their heads in contempt and hurled insults at Jesus. They mocked His earlier statement about destroying and rebuilding the temple in three days, challenging Him to prove He was God's Son by stepping down from the cross. Their taunts repeated Satan's temptation in the wilderness, urging Him to avoid the suffering needed to save others.

The chief priests, scribes, and elders gathered around the cross to mock Him as well. They sneered that He had claimed to save others by healing them, but now could not even save Himself from death. Their words held a profound truth they failed to see: if Jesus saved Himself, He could not save anyone else.

The religious leaders mocked Jesus' trust in God, demanding that God rescue Him immediately if He truly delighted in Him as His Son. Without knowing it, they quoted the exact words predicted in Psalm 22:8 for the enemies of the Messiah. They assumed His suffering meant God had rejected Him, but He was actually doing the Father's will.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox readers note that this mock challenge closely parallels Wisdom 2:13-20, an Old Testament book in their Bibles that describes ungodly men testing a righteous sufferer who calls himself a child of God.

notes.meaning: Even the two robbers hanging beside Jesus joined in insulting Him during the ordeal. Matthew records that both men initially hurled insults, though Luke tells us that one later repented and asked for mercy. Jesus endured mockery from every group present—rulers, bystanders, and dying criminals alike.
